articles.title: Probing the proteome at cellular scale
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02805-wRapid technological advances are allowing researchers to identify thousands of proteins in individual cells, revealing the hidden mechanisms underlying development and disease.
articles.content:
When a fertilized mammalian egg divides, it yields two seemingly identical daughter cells. Some of their descendants generate the diverse organ systems of the embryo, while others form extra-embryonic tissues that sustain the developmental process.

In 2025, researchers used a cutting-edge technique known as single-cell proteomics (SCP) to show that even in the two first-generation cells, this division of labour is already established1. Nikolai Slavov at Northeastern University in Boston, Massachusetts, who co-directed the study with fellow cell biologists Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz and Tsui-Fen Chou at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, says that the protein contents of these two cells, which were termed ‘alpha’ and ‘beta’, reveal distinct properties and fates. “Beta cells were more likely to give rise to healthy embryos than the alpha cells,” he says, whereas alpha cells typically formed extra-embryonic tissues. The team could trace these identities back to fertilization.

Where do proteins go in cells? Next-generation methods map the molecules’ hidden lives

Other questions are also yielding to the technology. Researchers now recognize, for instance, that many of the most clinically significant events in the formation of tumours originate from individual cells camouflaged in the chaotic tumour environment. “Single-cell proteomics may help us understand why patients have different outcomes due to tumour evolution, immune responses and cell differentiation — all driven by cellular heterogeneity,” says Yu-Ju Chen, a mass spectrometrist at Academia Sinica in Taipei.

Just a few years ago, protein biologists largely dismissed the possibility of single-cell proteomics — profiling thousands of proteins in individual cells — as the stuff of science fiction. “I’m almost on the record as saying, ‘not in my lifetime’, because it seemed to be so far off,” says Matthias Mann, a proteomics researcher at the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry in Martinsried, Germany. But over the past decade, SCP has become not only possible but practical — and scientifically informative. Mann himself is now an avid practitioner, using SCP to study illnesses ranging from liver conditions to Alzheimer’s disease. The bar to entry remains high, however, and the need for expensive equipment, deep expertise and methodological precision to process cell-scale volumes of protein still limits the potentially transformative impact of this technology.

Precious cargo

Biology is already deep in the single-cell era, but most such analyses focus on the transcriptome. Profiling gene expression at the level of the individual cell can provide valuable information about a cell’s identity or physiological state. But researchers cannot necessarily predict the protein contents of a cell from its RNA alone — not every RNA gets translated, and numerous factors shape the timing and extent of protein production from a given transcript. Many disease mechanisms can best be understood by surveying the protein contents — for example, the pathology of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease is strongly linked to aberrant aggregates of protein. “The proteome reflects the current state of the cell,” Mann says.

Focus on single-cell proteomics

To survey that state, proteomics researchers typically work in bulk, pooling and analysing thousands or millions of cells using mass spectrometry (MS). This technique uses specialized instruments that break samples down into ionized pieces, which are then analysed in terms of their mass and charge. The resulting ‘fingerprint’ enables precise identification of the molecule from which the fragment originated, and researchers can routinely detect 10,000 or more distinct proteins per sample. But this is an averaged perspective that can obscure the underlying biology. “Are they really reflecting what’s going on in all cells or is it just a small population of cells where you see dramatic changes?” asks Jesper Olsen, a mass spectrometrist at the University of Copenhagen. “These are things we have not really been able to address before.”

Enter single-cell proteomics

In some ways, the technology should be simpler than its transcriptomic analogue. Protein is more stable than RNA is, and more abundant. “With RNA, we count zero, one, two, three [copies] most of the time; with proteins, we count 100, 500, 10,000,” says Slavov. But transcriptomics researchers can boost the cellular RNA signal by using the PCR amplification technique. No such tool exists for the proteome, and researchers must learn all they can from a few hundred picograms of material.

Getting a robust and informative signal from such tiny quantities requires a highly sensitive mass spectrometer — but sample preparation poses a more formidable challenge. “The raw sensitivity was there … but the sample prep was optimized for bulk level,” says Ryan Kelly, a biochemist at Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah.

Matthias Mann’s Deep Visual Proteomics strategy adds spatial data to single-cell proteomics.Credit: Axel Griesch/Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry

In 2018, a team led by Slavov demonstrated an important first step towards broad proteomic coverage at the single-cell level2. The researchers developed a sample preparation and analysis workflow called SCoPE-MS (single-cell proteomics by mass spectrometry), in which they chemically labelled proteins in individual cells of interest and then mixed these with an excess of unlabelled ‘carrier’ cells. This limited protein loss from the target cells and made protein identification easier, enabling the detection of more than 1,500 proteins across eight individual cells. “We essentially gained about four orders of magnitude in sensitivity,” he says.

Slavov recalls that the publication of his results was met with scepticism, but other groups soon replicated them. And importantly, a second group led by Kelly published an independent approach to SCP that same year, using a sample preparation device called the nanoPOTS chip (nanodroplet processing in one pot for trace samples) to identify 670 proteins in small numbers of individual cells3. “The whole point of those early papers was, ‘this is real signal from single cells’,” says Kelly. “It’s not a question any more.”

A growing crowd

Since then, the field has advanced at a remarkable pace. Jennifer Van Eyk, a clinical proteomics researcher at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, California, says that her team has developed a workflow that can consistently identify 1,500–2,000 proteins per cell. “The biology we’re seeing is just unbelievable,” she says.

Proteomics sets up single-cell and single-molecule solutions

And deeper coverage is possible. In 2025, two independent studies inventoried more than 5,000 proteins per cell — a figure that is already being surpassed. Olsen, who led one study4, says his group has work under review in which they identify up to 7,000 proteins in individual cells. And Karl Mechtler, a proteomics researcher at the Research Institute of Molecular Pathology in Vienna, who co-directed the other study5, notes that with some larger cells, “you can get up to 8,000 or 9,000 proteins”.

Many SCP laboratories now rely on the cellenONE, a device commercialized by Cellenion in Lyon, France, that makes it possible to isolate individual cells from a culture or tissue sample while also imaging them. That allows users to record each cell’s shape and size, which matter because cells can vary considerably in volume and protein content.

Downstream processing steps have also been optimized, minimizing sample loss and preventing cross-contamination that could confound interpretation of the data. Although chemical labelling of proteins was a key step in Slavov’s 2018 publication, many groups have adopted unlabelled approaches that are simpler and faster. For example, Kelly’s team developed a single-step process in 2023 that remains its go-to protocol6. And Chen and her collaborator at Academia Sinica, Hsiung-Lin Tu, have integrated the full sample preparation process into a compact microfluidic device. Known as the SciProChip, it performs all the necessary steps in nanoscale volumes of liquid7. “The chip substantially improved our sensitivity, reproducibility and quantitation accuracy,” says Chen.

The SciProChip uses microfluidics to capture, count and process individual cells for analysis.Credit: Hsiung-Lin Tu and Yu-Ju Chen

Advances in MS instrumentation have also propelled the field. Popular options include the Orbitrap Astral machines from Thermo Fisher Scientific in Waltham, Massachusetts, and the timsTOF Ultra line from Bruker in Billerica, Massachusetts. These systems employ different strategies to detect and quantify proteins that would be invisible with older technology, but can cost around US$1 million. “We can quantify much more sensitively, much more deeply, and at high throughput even more proteins in single cells,” says Slavov. However, he notes that the more affordable, older-generation systems remain effective for profiling high-abundance proteins.

The biggest hurdle is speed. Most SCP pipelines top out at a few hundred cells per day — orders of magnitude lower than the throughput of transcriptomics studies. This is mainly because of the need to separate cellular peptides by size before MS analysis. Going faster can mean sacrificing precious data, says Kelly: “When we switch from 288 samples per day to 500 samples per day, we do see a big hit in our proteome coverage.”

Single-cell proteomics takes centre stage

Multiplexing offers one solution, in which individual cells are labelled such that the data from each can be disentangled even after the cells have been pooled for processing and analysis. For example, the labelling strategy Slavov used in 2018, based on MS-resolvable ‘tandem mass tags’, can resolve dozens of samples in parallel. But labelling adds complexity to sample preparation and can confound data analysis. “In the end, you end up getting actually quite a low identification rate from the peptides compared to a label-free experiment,” says Olsen.

This advancement has broad implications for understanding development, disease mechanisms, and personalized medicine, including cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. articles.personality_title: New technology reveals protein secrets inside single cells
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists want to understand how cells work by studying their proteins. Proteins are important because they do most of the jobs inside cells. Until recently, it was very hard to study proteins in just one cell because cells are so small and proteins are tiny.

**What happened** – In recent years, researchers developed a new method called single-cell proteomics (SCP). This method uses special machines called mass spectrometers to find and measure thousands of different proteins inside individual cells. In 2025, scientists showed that even the first two cells after a fertilized egg have different protein patterns that decide their future roles in the body. Many labs around the world have since improved this technology to identify up to 9,000 proteins in one cell.

**Impact** – This technology is important because it lets scientists see differences between cells that were hidden before. For example, in cancer, some single cells behave differently and cause the disease to grow or resist treatment. SCP helps researchers understand these differences better. It also helps study brain diseases like Alzheimer’s by showing which proteins are involved. This could lead to better treatments and understanding of many diseases.

**What's next step** – Scientists are working to make SCP faster and easier to use. Right now, it takes a long time and expensive equipment. New tools like tiny chips and better machines are being developed to speed up the process. Researchers hope that soon SCP will be used more widely in hospitals to study diseases at the level of single cells.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Single-cell proteomics is a new technology that lets scientists study thousands of proteins in individual cells, opening the door to better understanding and treating diseases.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle technologie révèle les secrets des protéines dans les cellules individuelles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques veulent comprendre comment fonctionnent les cellules en étudiant leurs protéines. Les protéines sont importantes car elles réalisent la plupart des tâches à l’intérieur des cellules. Jusqu’à récemment, il était très difficile d’étudier les protéines dans une seule cellule car elles sont très petites.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Ces dernières années, des chercheurs ont mis au point une nouvelle méthode appelée protéomique unicellulaire (PUC). Cette méthode utilise des machines spéciales appelées spectromètres de masse pour identifier et mesurer des milliers de protéines différentes dans des cellules individuelles. En 2025, des scientifiques ont montré que même les deux premières cellules après un œuf fécondé ont des profils de protéines différents qui déterminent leur rôle futur dans le corps. De nombreux laboratoires ont depuis amélioré cette technologie pour identifier jusqu’à 9 000 protéines dans une seule cellule.

**Impact** – Cette technologie est importante car elle permet aux scientifiques de voir des différences entre les cellules qui étaient cachées auparavant. Par exemple, dans le cancer, certaines cellules uniques se comportent différemment et font progresser la maladie ou résistent au traitement. La PUC aide à mieux comprendre ces différences. Elle aide aussi à étudier les maladies du cerveau comme Alzheimer en montrant quelles protéines sont impliquées. Cela pourrait conduire à de meilleurs traitements et à une meilleure compréhension de nombreuses maladies.

**Étape suivante** – Les scientifiques travaillent à rendre la PUC plus rapide et plus facile à utiliser. Pour l’instant, cela prend beaucoup de temps et nécessite du matériel coûteux. De nouveaux outils comme des puces microscopiques et de meilleures machines sont en développement pour accélérer le processus. Les chercheurs espèrent que bientôt la PUC sera largement utilisée dans les hôpitaux pour étudier les maladies au niveau des cellules individuelles.

**Message clé en une phrase** – La protéomique unicellulaire est une nouvelle technologie qui permet d’étudier des milliers de protéines dans chaque cellule, ouvrant la voie à une meilleure compréhension et traitement des maladies.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva tecnología revela los secretos de las proteínas dentro de células individuales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos quieren entender cómo funcionan las células estudiando sus proteínas. Las proteínas son importantes porque realizan la mayoría de las funciones dentro de las células. Hasta hace poco, era muy difícil estudiar las proteínas en una sola célula porque son muy pequeñas.

**Qué pasó** – En los últimos años, los investigadores desarrollaron un método llamado proteómica unicelular (PU). Este método usa máquinas especiales llamadas espectrómetros de masa para identificar y medir miles de proteínas diferentes dentro de células individuales. En 2025, los científicos demostraron que incluso las dos primeras células después de un óvulo fertilizado tienen patrones de proteínas diferentes que deciden sus futuros roles en el cuerpo. Muchos laboratorios han mejorado esta tecnología para identificar hasta 9,000 proteínas en una sola célula.

**Impacto** – Esta tecnología es importante porque permite a los científicos ver diferencias entre las células que antes estaban ocultas. Por ejemplo, en el cáncer, algunas células únicas se comportan diferente y causan que la enfermedad crezca o resista el tratamiento. La PU ayuda a entender mejor estas diferencias. También ayuda a estudiar enfermedades cerebrales como el Alzheimer mostrando qué proteínas están involucradas. Esto podría llevar a mejores tratamientos y entendimiento de muchas enfermedades.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos están trabajando para hacer la PU más rápida y fácil de usar. Ahora mismo, toma mucho tiempo y equipo caro. Se están desarrollando nuevas herramientas como chips pequeños y mejores máquinas para acelerar el proceso. Los investigadores esperan que pronto la PU se use más en hospitales para estudiar enfermedades a nivel de células individuales.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La proteómica unicelular es una nueva tecnología que permite estudiar miles de proteínas en células individuales, abriendo la puerta a un mejor entendimiento y tratamiento de enfermedades.

articles.title: UK pupils score highly in international tests despite global slump in reading
articles.summary: But the Pisa test scores vary significantly between England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
articles.content:
UK pupils have performed well again in international science, reading and maths tests sat every three years by hundreds of thousands of teenagers around the world.

The UK's performance in the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) remained steady, ranking below the highest-performing countries like Singapore, Estonia and parts of China, but ahead of the US, Australia and other major European nations.

But the Pisa report also warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills.

England's schools minister, Georgia Gould, said the government wanted to "build on" the positive results and "go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy".

The Pisa tests, run by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), assess teenagers on their ability to solve problems, think critically and communicate, before asking them a wider range of questions about their education in a questionnaire.

Although the UK performed well overall, the rankings varied significantly again, with results showing England, where the curriculum is significantly different, pulling consistently ahead of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on UK pupils performing well in international assessments of science, reading, and maths, indicating positive educational outcomes which have broad societal benefits. Despite a global decline in reading skills, the UK's steady performance and government commitment to improving literacy and numeracy highlight meaningful progress in education, a key factor in health and well-being. The story is focused, provides context, and discusses significant educational achievements impacting many young people.
articles.personality_title: UK pupils maintain strong international test scores despite global reading decline
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every three years, teenagers around the world take tests called Pisa to measure their skills in reading, science, and maths. These tests help show how well different countries are teaching young people.

**What happened** – In the latest Pisa tests, UK pupils scored well overall. While countries like Singapore and Estonia ranked highest, the UK ranked ahead of countries such as the US and Australia. However, the results differed within the UK: England's students scored better than those in Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales.

**Impact** – The UK’s steady performance is important because it shows that many young people are learning key skills like problem-solving and critical thinking. This is especially notable as reading skills are dropping worldwide. The government plans to use these results to improve literacy and numeracy even more, helping students leave school better prepared.

**What's next step** – The UK government aims to build on these results by focusing on stronger teaching and support in schools. This could lead to higher reading and maths skills across all parts of the UK, reducing the differences between England and the other nations.

**One-sentence takeaway** – UK pupils continue to perform well in global tests, and the government plans to improve education to help all students succeed.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les élèves britanniques maintiennent de bons résultats aux tests internationaux malgré la baisse mondiale en lecture
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Tous les trois ans, des adolescents du monde entier passent des tests appelés Pisa pour mesurer leurs compétences en lecture, sciences et maths. Ces tests montrent la qualité de l’enseignement dans chaque pays.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Lors des derniers tests Pisa, les élèves britanniques ont obtenu de bons résultats. Bien que des pays comme Singapour et l’Estonie soient en tête, le Royaume-Uni se place devant des pays comme les États-Unis et l’Australie. Cependant, les résultats varient à l’intérieur du Royaume-Uni : les élèves d’Angleterre ont obtenu de meilleurs scores que ceux d’Irlande du Nord, d’Écosse et du Pays de Galles.

**Impact** – La performance stable du Royaume-Uni est importante car elle montre que beaucoup de jeunes acquièrent des compétences clés comme la résolution de problèmes et la pensée critique. Cela est d’autant plus notable que les compétences en lecture baissent dans le monde. Le gouvernement souhaite utiliser ces résultats pour améliorer encore la lecture et les maths, afin que les élèves quittent l’école mieux préparés.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement britannique veut s’appuyer sur ces résultats en renforçant l’enseignement et le soutien dans les écoles. Cela pourrait augmenter les compétences en lecture et maths dans tout le Royaume-Uni, en réduisant les écarts entre l’Angleterre et les autres nations.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les élèves britanniques réussissent bien aux tests mondiaux, et le gouvernement veut améliorer l’éducation pour que tous les élèves réussissent.
articles.personality_title_es: Los alumnos del Reino Unido mantienen buenos resultados en pruebas internacionales a pesar de la caída global en lectura
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada tres años, adolescentes de todo el mundo realizan pruebas llamadas Pisa para medir sus habilidades en lectura, ciencias y matemáticas. Estas pruebas muestran qué tan bien enseñan los países a sus jóvenes.

**Qué pasó** – En las últimas pruebas Pisa, los alumnos del Reino Unido obtuvieron buenos resultados. Aunque países como Singapur y Estonia lideran, el Reino Unido quedó por delante de países como Estados Unidos y Australia. Sin embargo, los resultados varían dentro del Reino Unido: los estudiantes de Inglaterra obtuvieron mejores puntajes que los de Irlanda del Norte, Escocia y Gales.

**Impacto** – El buen desempeño del Reino Unido es importante porque indica que muchos jóvenes están aprendiendo habilidades clave como resolver problemas y pensar críticamente. Esto es especialmente relevante ya que las habilidades de lectura están bajando en todo el mundo. El gobierno planea usar estos resultados para mejorar aún más la lectura y las matemáticas, ayudando a que los estudiantes terminen la escuela mejor preparados.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno del Reino Unido quiere aprovechar estos resultados para fortalecer la enseñanza y el apoyo en las escuelas. Esto podría elevar las habilidades en lectura y matemáticas en todas las regiones, reduciendo las diferencias entre Inglaterra y las otras naciones.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los alumnos del Reino Unido continúan teniendo buenos resultados en pruebas globales y el gobierno planea mejorar la educación para que todos los estudiantes tengan éxito.
